overview: This 1100 to 1200 map record represents the historical Artsakh region and the world of Khachen’s local princes, monasteries and settlements. It is not a modern state boundary. Archaeology at Tigranakert and dated Armenian inscriptions reveal both ordinary work and the institutions of powerful families.

periods.title: Settlements and local lordships
periods.summary: The medieval Khachen landscape included fortified centers and an inhabited Tigranakert, whose houses and pottery reveal substantial urban activity.

periods.title: Law and learned patronage
periods.summary: Mkhitar Gosh’s legal writing was associated with Haterk’s princely household in 1184, linking scholarship with local patronage.

sections.title: The historical region and the imperfect outline

items.text: The imported outline includes Tigranakert, Handaberd and Amaras, but excludes Dadivank and Gandzasar. Those excluded monasteries still provide evidence for historical Khachen. Their examples are located explicitly below. This coarse polygon is neither a verified medieval frontier nor evidence for modern sovereignty, and neighboring Armenia and Arran have separate records.

At Dadivank, outside this outline, Hasan son of Vakhtang left an inscription dated 1182. He names six sons and says he gave them his fortresses and districts before becoming a religious in the monastery near his brother Grigores. Family inheritance and religious retirement appear in the same political document.

Tigranakert’s Central Quarter changed repeatedly. Houses built between the eleventh and mid-twelfth centuries had clay floors, substantial pits and clay-lined tonir ovens as much as 1.5 metres across. The remains bring us into working rooms, where preparing food and storing supplies occupied real space.

By the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, another Tigranakert complex had partly sunken rooms, narrow passages and light reed roofs supported on wooden posts. Its smaller ovens and shallow hearths show a different arrangement of domestic work. A town’s houses did not all follow one timeless plan.

An iron chopping knife from Tigranakert is dated to the eleventh or twelfth century and interpreted as a tool for gardening and cutting bushes. Excavators also found worn whetstones for sharpening blades. Keeping a useful edge was part of the job; a tool needed care between its turns at work.

A mill’s upper runner stone from Tigranakert is also dated to the eleventh or twelfth century. The excavation report describes mortars whose bases were worn down through repeated grinding. Grain processing left its mark on the stone itself, turning a household chore into something archaeologists can recognize centuries later.

A complete storage jar was found on a twelfth-century floor at Tigranakert. Excavators interpret it as a grain container. Large pottery vessels helped households keep provisions together; alongside the ovens and grinding tools, this jar supplies another piece of the journey from harvested grain to a meal.

Some Tigranakert plates from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries carry birds, animals and plant ornament under their glaze. Not every table was plain brown pottery. One fragment shows a bird that researchers identify cautiously as an eagle or peacock: even a fancy broken plate can keep a small mystery.

Glass bracelets from Tigranakert’s broader ninth- to thirteenth-century layers include blue, green and black examples, with occasional multicolored pieces. Their fragments record personal adornment as well as the practical vessels of a household. They cannot tell us the names, ages or genders of all the people who wore them.

Tigranakert’s canal combined open channels with rock-cut passages and tunnels. Investigators excavated a 300-metre rock-cut stretch and found limestone laid to reduce water loss. They interpret the older canal as remaining in use into the thirteenth century for irrigation and domestic needs. This was inherited water infrastructure, not a newly invented twelfth-century system.

sections.title: Books, learning and a voice in Armenian

items.text: The scholar Mkhitar Gosh spent several years with Prince Vakhtang and his brothers in Khachen. He had studied in different centers and later taught others. His career shows how a princely household could support a traveling scholar, connecting this region with a much wider Armenian intellectual world.

Gosh began his Lawcode in 1184. It addressed secular as well as church matters and influenced later Armenian legal collections, including those in Cilicia and communities farther away. Writing rules down was a major intellectual project; the existence of a code does not mean every local dispute was settled exactly as its author wished.

A manuscript associated with Gosh’s legal work was made for Haterk’s Prince Vakhtang and his wife Arzukhatun in 1184. A later inscription from Khadavank, dated 1204 and preserved in the Matenadaran, records a manuscript library. This small step beyond the map’s endpoint shows the continuation of organized book collecting.

A short Armenian sample from Dadivank’s 1182 stone is ԵՍ ՀԱՍԱՆ, transliterated Es Hasan, meaning “I, Hasan.” These are the opening words after its date in the published transcription. Modern type preserves the wording, rather than reproducing the shape of the carved letters.

In Gosh’s fable 168, gold declares itself king and expects other materials to bow. Wheat refuses: in a famine, even gold must come asking for food. This is a story, not an account of talking crops, but it makes the value of farmers’ work wonderfully difficult to overlook.

Another Gosh fable tells of a healthy man who mocks physicians, then changes his mind after becoming ill. Gosh compares bodily care with listening to spiritual teachers. The tale shows medicine as a familiar subject for moral instruction; it does not document a particular clinic or treatment in Khachen.

The celebrated Gandzasar church belongs to the following century, outside both this record’s dates and its coarse outline. Hasan Jalal commissioned it between 1216 and 1238, and it was consecrated in 1240. Its inscriptions name family members and patrons, preserving the relationships behind an ambitious building project.

Under Mongol pressure in the thirteenth century, Hasan Jalal combined resistance, submission and diplomacy to preserve his position. He traveled to Mongol rulers, but was ultimately killed in 1260 or 1261. His descendants continued as patrons and builders. Political accommodation could preserve institutions for a time without making their leaders secure.

ending.text: The atlas stops this label in 1200, not at the disappearance of Khachen’s communities. Princely patronage and Armenian religious and literary life continued into later centuries, under changing rulers and pressures. The thirteenth-century story of Hasan Jalal demonstrates continuity alongside a major loss of political security.
